answer: Frontier multimodal LLMs (and text-only LLMs on the text subset) are the objects of evaluation. Table 1 evaluates GPT-4o, Grok 2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, o1, DeepSeek-R1 and o3-mini.

The intended use is to measure frontier LLM capability on closed-ended academic questions, serving as a common reference point for AI progress. The stated users are researchers, scientists and policymakers. It is also meant to replace saturated benchmarks such as MMLU. The paper says it is not a measure of autonomous research or AGI.

The paper does not define a fine-grained capability taxonomy. The capability of interest is broad expert-level academic capability on closed-ended questions at the frontier of human knowledge. This includes technical knowledge and reasoning, with an emphasis on deep mathematical reasoning. Calibration (confidence matching accuracy) is a second measured property. The context is closed-ended, verifiable, short-answer or multiple-choice questions. The paper says HLE does not test open-ended research or creativity.

The creators link the capability to the use by arguing that saturated benchmarks limit precise measurement, so a harder benchmark is needed to track frontier progress and inform policy. They say high performance would suggest expert-level capability on closed-ended academic questions. The paper does not discuss whether the capabilities are theoretically attainable by LLMs. It implies they are, since it expects rapid progress and says models could exceed 50% by the end of 2025.

The sources give little validity evidence for the choice and definition of capabilities. They offer only the motivation of saturation on MMLU (Figure 1) and the claim that a broad expert-written question set tests academic capability. They give no construct validation, such as correlation with other measures or expert-human baselines.

The benchmark has 2,500 public questions in over a hundred subjects, including math (emphasized), humanities, natural sciences, CS/AI, engineering and trivia. About 14% need text plus an image. 24% are multiple choice (five or more options) and the rest are exact-match. Each submission includes question, answer, rationale, subject and contributor. Questions are original, graduate-level or highly specific, non-searchable, and answered with short strings. Items are not mapped to separate capabilities; every item targets general expert academic knowledge and reasoning.

The creators say items elicit evidence by being precise, unambiguous, closed-ended questions with a known verifiable answer and a rationale. Items are non-searchable and require expert knowledge. Contributors modify parameters, such as the number of answer choices, to discourage lucky guesses and correct answers with faulty reasoning. The justification is by design rules and not by an item-level analysis of the capability each item elicits.

The creators offer a multi-stage review as content-validity evidence. Questions must first stump frontier LLMs. They then pass two rounds of expert review with rubrics, with each question getting 1-3 reviews. A public bug bounty and student audits followed. A removal of searchable questions was also done. Two audits of 200 questions each estimated expert disagreement at 15.4% on the public set, and about 18% on a bio/chem/health subset. The paper admits that reviewers were not expected to verify solutions that would take more than five minutes.

Models receive the question, with an image for multimodal items. A standardized system prompt asks for an Explanation, an Answer and a Confidence (0–100%). The prompt is zero-shot with chain-of-thought-style reasoning. Models without system-prompt support get it as a user prompt. The temperature is 0.0 where configurable. The repository README advises max completion tokens of at least 8192 for reasoning models. A separate document describes a web+code tool setting for HLE-Diamond.

The paper gives limited justification. It says the standardized prompt structures reasoning followed by an answer. It handles non-multimodal models by evaluating them on the text-only subset. It handles models without system-prompt support by using a user prompt. It reports text-only results for all models in the appendix. It does not discuss prompt sensitivity or suitability across model families. Temperature differs for o1 and o3-mini (1.0) and for Gemini Flash Thinking (0.7).

The sources give no validity evidence for the adaptation choice. They do not report ablations over prompts, prompt-sensitivity checks, or comparisons with other elicitation formats. The only related notes are the temperature and token-limit settings and the observed model collapse, which led to the max-token recommendation.

The 2,500 questions of the public set are all used. A private held-out set is kept to detect overfitting. About 13,000 questions that stumped LLMs went to expert review from over 70,000 logged attempts. The final selection was based on difficulty (models failing), reviewer scores, organizer approval, searchability audits and audit-driven fixes. Late contributions form a second private set. HLE-Rolling is a planned dynamic fork.

The paper does not show that assembly ensures sufficient evidence for each capability. It claims broad coverage across dozens or hundreds of subjects and an emphasis on math. Subjects were self-declared by contributors. There is no capability-wise sufficiency argument.

The validity evidence for assembly is limited. The paper says searchable-question filtering did not change frontier-model performance much. It reports a private held-out set to assess overfitting. It also states that adversarial LLM filtering is deliberately not strong, so non-zero accuracy remains. There are no other assembly validations, such as the effect of the LLM-based difficulty filter on model rankings.

For each item, the model's full response is captured, with its explanation, final answer and stated confidence. An LLM judge (o3-mini, with structured decoding) extracts the final answer, a reasoning note, a yes/no correctness decision and the confidence from that response. The result is a binary correct flag with a confidence value. Multiple-choice and exact-match answers are both compared with the reference answer.

The creators argue that answers are short, closed-ended and unambiguous, so a matching judgment shows whether the model got the expert-verified answer right. They also argue the judge handles equivalent formats such as decimals and fractions. Confidence extraction is used for calibration. They do not argue in detail how a correct answer reflects deeper reasoning, as opposed to guessing or memorization.

The sources offer no validation of the LLM judge, such as agreement with human graders or error rates. The only related evidence is the estimated expert disagreement rate of the labels (15.4%, about 18% for a health subset), which concerns the reference answers and not the extraction. The judge code comments say judge failures are 'very, very rare' with no data. The paper notes that exact match can give false negatives during review.

Per-item correctness is aggregated into accuracy over the questions, reported overall and by category (Math, Bio/Med, Physics, CS/AI, Humanities, Chemistry, Engineering, Other). Calibration is reported as RMS calibration error using binned confidence (bin size 100). Average completion tokens are also reported. The repository adds a Wald 95% interval for accuracy. There is no aggregate capability score beyond accuracy and calibration.

The creators say low accuracy shows a gap with expert-level capability and high accuracy would suggest expert-level performance. They say high calibration error shows models do not recognize their uncertainty. Per-category breakdowns are reported. They state that small accuracy changes near zero are not strongly indicative of progress. The link between accuracy on this set and general academic capability is asserted and not argued in detail.

The validity evidence for accumulation is thin. The paper reports category-wise results and a text-only comparison. The code gives a confidence interval for accuracy. It cites existing calibration implementations. There is no analysis of metric reliability, and no human expert baseline for the accuracy scale.
BIASED (questions are selected to stump frontier LLMs and come from volunteer contributors, so they are not a representative sample of academic knowledge)
PARTIAL (adversarially filtered against specific frontier LLMs, so those models are disadvantaged. Questions are in English, with an academic and Western-institution contributor skew.)
The objects of evaluation are code-generating language models (Codex, Codex-S, GPT-3, GPT-J, GPT-Neo, Tabnine), assessed on Python function synthesis from docstrings.

Intended use: measure functional correctness of program synthesis from docstrings, and let others evaluate problem-solving capabilities of their models. Intended users are implicitly researchers/model developers; not explicitly named.

Capabilities named loosely: language comprehension, reasoning, algorithms, simple mathematics; overall functional-correctness code writing from docstrings. No formal definitions of each capability. Limitations section discusses long chains of operations and variable binding via separate synthetic tests.
Paper motivates via Copilot-style practical use and test-driven developer practice; attainability shown by nonzero pass rates. No explicit argument linking each capability to the use.
No validity evidence for the choice or definition of capabilities; the paper offers only the argument for functional correctness and that problems are comparable to easy interview questions.

164 hand-written Python problems, each with function signature, docstring, body, and several unit tests (avg 7.7). Difficulty ranges from easy to hard; capability mapping per item is not given beyond the broad list.
Items elicit evidence by requiring a model to complete a function that must pass unit tests; hand-writing is meant to avoid training contamination. No per-item justification of targeted capabilities.

Little content validity evidence: problems hand-written, not programmatically copied (though not a guarantee of novelty); several unit tests per problem. No expert review, test coverage analysis, or error audit reported.

Models receive a prompt of header, signature and docstring and sample completions until stop sequences ('
class','
def','
#','
if','
print'), with nucleus sampling top p 0.95 and tuned temperature. Zero-shot for HumanEval; 1-shot hint for APPS.

No explicit justification of suitability across all models; temperature is tuned per k, and for GPT-Neo/J best of several temperatures used. Docstring-completion format suits code-trained models; suitability for general models not discussed.
Evidence limited to showing temperature affects pass@k (Fig 5) and that stop sequences prevent extra code. No comparison with alternative prompt formats.
All 164 problems are used; n=200 samples per task, k≤100. No subset selection described.
No argument that the full set gives sufficient evidence per capability; capabilities are not separately sampled.
No validity evidence for assembly; only the unbiased pass@k estimator with n samples is justified to reduce variance.
Generated completions are executed against unit tests in a sandbox; per sample pass/fail is captured (README: passed, timed out, failed). Evidence is the count c of correct samples out of n.
Argued that functional correctness is what developers use and that match metrics like BLEU poorly separate correct and incorrect solutions. No further link to individual capabilities.
Evidence: BLEU overlap analysis (Fig 8) vs correctness, and README sanity check with example samples. No test-suite adequacy or false-pass analysis.
Per-problem pass@k computed with the unbiased estimator and averaged over problems; reported by model size and temperature. Also best-of-k selection by log-probability.
Aggregate pass@k is treated as overall problem-solving capability; no decomposition by capability. Separate synthetic experiments probe chain length.
Evidence is a proof that the estimator is unbiased (Appendix A) and a comparison with the biased 1−(1−p̂)^k (Fig 13). No validity evidence that pass@k reflects the capabilities.
CAPABILITY (Python function synthesis from docstrings / problem-solving)
BIASED (164 hand-written, mostly easy interview-style problems in Python only, with simple algorithms and math)
PARTIAL (Python only, English docstrings, and a prompt format with stop sequences and few-shot-free completion suited to code-trained language models)

The objects of evaluation are language agents, meaning LMs used with an agent method such as function calling, ReAct or Act. The agents get domain API tools and a policy document. Models tested include gpt-4o, claude-3-opus, gemini-1.5 and llama-3-70B.

The use is to evaluate and develop agents for real-world deployment, in particular customer-service-like settings with human interaction and rule following. It is also meant for comparing models and methods and for testing reliability across repeated trials. The intended users are researchers and developers of agents, models, tool use and dialogue. The code is released for the community to extend. Users are not named as a formal category.

Three desiderata are the capabilities of interest. (1) Interacting with humans and APIs over long horizons to gather information and resolve intents. (2) Accurately following complex domain-specific policies and rules. (3) Consistency and reliability across many trials, measured by pass^k. The paper also mentions long-context reasoning, planning, database reasoning and handling compound requests. They are defined informally and in the customer-service retail and airline contexts. They have no formal operational definitions.

The paper links the capabilities to deployment as follows. Deployment requires these desiderata, and existing benchmarks lack human interaction and policy following. It does not explicitly argue that the capabilities are theoretically attainable. It treats them as open challenges and notes the tasks are not solved by current agents. It also says it chose retail and airline because they are close to real-world applications.

The creators offer little formal validity evidence for the choice of capabilities. They offer an argument from related work and real-world needs. They give a policy-removal ablation, which suggests policy following matters in the airline domain. They also give a failure analysis in which they manually examine failures. There are no expert surveys, no correlation with real deployments and no construct validity studies.

Test items are tasks. Each pairs a user-simulator instruction (identity, intent and preferences, hidden from the agent) with ground-truth database write actions and optionally required output strings. There are 115 retail tasks and 50 airline tasks. They are conversational and multi-turn, over JSON databases, Python API tools and Markdown policies. Each task is designed to have a single unique outcome. The paper does not map each task to a specific capability. Every task is aimed jointly at interaction, rule following and (via repeated trials) reliability.

Items elicit evidence through multi-turn dialogue with an LM user. The agent has to gather information, call tools and obey policy rules, for example refusing a basic economy change, collecting all exchange items into one call, or computing prices. The database end state shows whether the agent made the correct decisions. The paper says tasks are diverse, open-ended and chosen for quality over quantity, and it gives examples. Some policy rules are enforced by the APIs and others are not. The argument is qualitative.

The evidence is as follows. Tasks were manually annotated and iteratively refined with gpt-4-turbo agent runs. Each retail task got more than 40 gpt-4-turbo trials, and tasks with zero or low success were checked. The paper reports a manual failure analysis: of 40 failed trajectories, 4 were due to instruction typos or ambiguity, which were then fixed. The authors acknowledge possible bias from tuning on the gpt-4-turbo agent. There are no independent annotator or expert reviews, no inter-annotator agreement, and no coverage analysis. The README warns that the tasks in this repository are outdated and not fixed, which implies later-found errors.

The agent gets the domain policy as its system prompt and the tool/function definitions. It interacts turn by turn with the LM user simulator (gpt-4-0613 in the paper). At each turn it either calls a tool or sends a user message. Methods include function calling, ReAct and Act-only. Agent temperature is 0.0 and user temperature 1.0. Each task is limited to at most 30 agent actions, and the episode ends when the user emits ###STOP###. The README documents the other user strategies (react, verify, reflection).

The paper gives limited justification. Function calling is natively supported by all tested models except Llama-3, so Llama-3 is run with text-ReAct. Small models were not tested because of difficulty. Methods like self-reflection and planning were considered unsuitable for a real-time user-in-the-loop setting. It reports that function calling outperforms text-formatted methods. This shows that the adaptation affects scores, which weakens comparisons across models that use different methods. The paper does not discuss whether the policy-as-system-prompt format suits all models.

The evidence is empirical comparison. It covers FC vs ReAct vs Act, a test of adding a think function, which did not help, and a policy-removal ablation. There are no sensitivity analyses on prompts, and no check of whether the user simulator model choice affects results. The paper does not report one.

The full set is used with no sampling. It has 115 retail tasks and 50 airline tasks (165 total). The repository splits the retail tasks into dev, train and test files. The paper says nothing about selecting a subset. The sizes follow from the cost and effort of manual annotation: it says it trades quantity for quality and that running a runs is costly (about $200 per trial per task set). At least 3 trials per task are run for the main results.

The paper does not say how assembly ensures sufficient evidence for each capability. The only related argument is that the domains permit diverse tasks and that the task difficulty spectrum is balanced (Figure 7). Figure 6 shows compound requests are harder. No coverage analysis for each capability is reported.

The creators offer no validity evidence for the assembly. They state a preference for a small high-quality task set and show that multiple trials reveal insights. Table 2 and Figure 4 report model differences, but there is no statistical analysis of whether the task count is enough. They state they report error bars in the checklist, but no error bars are visible in the text.

For each task, the final database state and the agent-to-user messages are captured. Evidence is extracted by rule-based comparison. raction is 1 if the final database equals the database produced by applying the ground truth write actions. routput is 1 if the agent's replies contain all required output strings as substrings. The reward is the product of the two, r in {0,1}. Read actions and dialogue wording are not scored directly.

The authors argue that, because each task has one possible outcome under policy and user desires, the database comparison replaces noisy human judgment. It captures decision making, rule following and information delivery via the end state. They admit that r=1 may be necessary but not sufficient. For example, the agent might issue a return without explicit user confirmation, which violates policy. They also admit that the user simulator may give incomplete knowledge or make errors. The reward does not capture some of the capabilities (the quality of conversation, some policy violations).

The support is limited. Task instructions were iterated so that outcomes are unique (more than 40 gpt-4-turbo trials per retail task). A manual examination of 40 gpt-4o failures found 4 due to instruction typo or ambiguity, the rest being agent issues. The paper calls the reward fast and faithful but gives no comparison with human judgment. It states that it did not use LM checks of rule following. No evidence is given for the airline domain beyond the general procedure.

Binary per-task rewards are averaged across tasks and trials. The default metric is pass^1, the mean reward. For consistency, pass^k is the chance that all k i.i.d. trials succeed, averaged across tasks, estimated as E_task[C(c,k)/C(n,k)]. pass@k is also given for contrast. Domain scores are averaged with equal domain weighting, not per task. Failures are broken down manually into categories, and results are split by domain and by number of write actions.

The pass^k metric is argued to capture reliability, because the same task is rerun with the same user prompt and database and only LM sampling varies. This tests whether the agent handles conversation variations with the same semantics. The pass^1 average captures overall task success. No metric separates information gathering, rule following and reliability from each other. Only the manual failure analysis and the policy ablation offer a capability-level view.

The paper shows that pass^k falls quickly as k grows (pass^8 < 25% for gpt-4o in retail) while pass@k rises. This supports pass^k being sensitive to inconsistency. It has no validation of pass^k against real deployment reliability and no analysis of uncertainty in the estimates (the checklist says error bars were reported but none appear in the text). The README leaderboard reports pass^1 to pass^4.
TASK-PERFORMANCE (customer-service tasks with tools, policy and simulated user)
BIASED (two customer-service domains, retail and airline, with simplified schemas; 115 and 50 tasks tuned using a gpt-4-turbo agent)
PARTIAL-INTERFERENCE (the simulated user is an external LLM API, gpt-4-0613 in the paper, and agents are called through APIs, so outcomes can vary with model versions and sampling)
COUPLED (the agent interacts with an LLM-simulated user and with tools and databases)
PARTIAL (task instructions were tuned using gpt-4-turbo agent runs, and gpt-4 was the user simulator and data generator, which may favour OpenAI models)

The objects of evaluation are language models, mainly pretrained text generators evaluated zero-shot. The paper tests GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2 and UnifiedQA (T5-based). Newer models (Anthropic, InstructGPT, WebGPT, Gopher) were evaluated externally.

The benchmark is meant to quantify how truthful models are, in the zero-shot setting. It is intended to help produce more truthful models and to understand the risks of deceptive ones. The users are implicitly ML researchers and developers. The authors also warn against over-reading results: strong performance does not imply truthfulness in specialised domains. They say it is unlikely to help build deceptive models.

The capability of interest is truthfulness: avoiding false statements, specifically imitative falsehoods learned from human text. Truth is defined strictly as the literal truth about the real world. Truthful means the answer avoids asserting a false statement, so refusals and 'No comment' count as true. Informativeness is a secondary dimension, defined as providing information that reduces the uncertainty raised by the question. The definition is given for zero-shot general-knowledge questions.

The creators link truthfulness to the concerns of accidental misuse, blocked positive applications and malicious misuse. They say truthfulness is necessary where models are deployed. They say models are not expected to be truthful under imitation objectives, but that larger models are more capable in principle of being both truthful and informative. They note that questions resemble real-world ones but were not collected from a deployed system. They concede that results may over- or under-estimate truthfulness for a deployed system.

The validity evidence is limited. The authors cite related work (Evans et al., 2021) for the concept. They justify a strict standard by analogy to scientific articles and Wikipedia. They distinguish truthfulness from related concepts. They run tests to separate imitative from non-imitative weaknesses: consistency across GPT-Neo/J, matched controls and paraphrases. They acknowledge that more semantic non-imitative weaknesses are harder to rule out.

The test set has 817 questions written by the authors, mostly one sentence with a median of 9 words. They cover 38 categories (health, law, finance, politics, fiction, misconceptions and others). Each question has sets of true and false reference answers and a supporting source. The questions are designed to elicit imitative falsehoods. 437 were adversarially filtered against GPT-3-175B and 380 were not filtered. Every item targets truthfulness, with informativeness measured on the answers.

Questions are written so that some humans would answer falsely from misconceptions, so a model that imitates human text is likely to produce a false answer. Adversarial filtering against GPT-3 selects items that elicit failures. Reference answers and sources let the answers be checked against the truth. The authors admit the adversarial procedure may also exploit non-imitative weaknesses such as syntax.

Two external researchers validated the items. A validator saw 100 random questions with one true and one false reference answer each and disagreed on 7%. A participant answered 250 questions and 6% of their answers were marked false. The authors suspect that part of this was mistakes by the external researchers, and they estimate disagreement at 2-6%. They modified 43 questions (5.3%) to reduce ambiguity. Control and paraphrase experiments test item validity. The README says a full validation of the remaining questions and sources has not been completed after the January 2025 updates.

The generation task is zero-shot. The model gets a prompt plus the question and writes a full-sentence answer using greedy decoding (temperature zero). The default is the QA prompt of trivia examples. No prompt is used for UnifiedQA. Other prompts (helpful, harmful, chat, long-form, null) are tested on GPT-3-175B. In the multiple-choice task, models score the likelihood of each reference answer given the prompt and question. The README describes a 1-2 sentence answer. The newer binary version shows two options (A)/(B) in random order.

The authors recommend true zero-shot with their prompts and hyperparameters for comparison. They argue few-shot would overstate truthfulness. A trivia prompt dissimilar to TruthfulQA is used for all models except UnifiedQA, which is already fine-tuned for QA. A multiple-choice variant is added so that models that are costly to evaluate can be assessed cheaply. They show that prompt choice strongly affects truthfulness, and that results agree across the generation and multiple-choice tasks. There is no systematic argument for suitability across all intended models, such as chat models.

The creators offer some evidence. The concordance between generation and multiple-choice results suggests that the inverse scaling is not an artifact of the hyperparameters. They test higher sampling temperatures (Appendix B.8), various prompts and paraphrased questions, and results show similar trends. These are robustness checks and not a direct validation of the adaptation choices.

All 817 questions are used as the test set. No subset is sampled. The question set was fixed during construction: 437 filtered and 380 unfiltered, with results reported on the combination. The results on the separate subsets are in Appendix B.4. The factors that shaped the set were the aim of eliciting imitative falsehoods, topic diversity across 38 categories, and the filtering against GPT-3. Human evaluation was costly, so some analyses use a subset of models or other methods.

The assembly was not designed to guarantee evidence for sub-capabilities. Diversity across 38 categories is the stated aim, so that a truthful model is truthful regardless of the topic. The authors say shallow coverage of general-knowledge topics is what the set offers. They report results by category and show that the best model was below the human average on almost all categories. The set mixes categories with very different numbers of questions, with some small.

The creators offer little direct support. They show per-category results (Appendix B.5), results on filtered versus unfiltered subsets (B.4), and consistency across model families. They mention a distribution of truthful models per question (B.7). There is no validation of the choice of how many questions or how the categories were chosen.

For generation, the model's full-sentence answer is captured. Human evaluators (the authors) blindly assign one of 13 qualitative labels, each mapped to a fixed scalar truth score, with a threshold of 0.5 for binary truth. A similar scheme is used for informativeness. The automated GPT-judge and GPT-info (GPT-3-6.7B fine-tuned) classify answers as true or false and informative. ROUGE, BLEURT and BLEU compare answers with reference answers. For multiple-choice, the likelihood of each reference answer is captured. The score is the normalized total likelihood of the true answers (MC2) or accuracy on the single-true choice (MC1).

A truthful answer is one that avoids asserting a false statement, and the evaluation scores it against sources and reference answers. Informativeness is scored separately so that evasive answers do not score well. The creators note that an answer such as 'No comment' is perfectly truthful, which is why the pair of scores is used. The automated metrics are trained to reproduce human labels. The reference answers cannot cover all statements models generate.

The evidence is substantial. GPT-judge predicts human evaluations with 90-96% validation accuracy on held-out model families, 90% on UnifiedQA when trained only on GPT answers, and 89.5% on the human baseline. GPT-info reaches 86.3% on UnifiedQA. GPT-judge is compared with ROUGE1 and BLEURT and outperforms them. Human evaluation uses a blinded procedure with a fixed label-to-score mapping. The authors report that GPT-judge misclassifies longer answers (Table 3) and say human evaluation remains the gold standard. Disagreement with the reference labels is estimated at 2-6%. There is no inter-annotator agreement among the evaluators, who were the authors.

The scores are accumulated per model by averaging over all questions: the percentage of answers judged true, the percentage informative and the percentage both true and informative. The scalar truth score average and the truth-times-info average are also reported. Results are compared across model sizes, prompts and families, and against the human baseline. Category breakdowns are given. For multiple-choice, the mean MC1 and MC2 scores are used.

Averaging the truthfulness and informativeness percentages reflects how often a model avoids false statements across diverse questions. Reporting both guards against gaming by non-committal answers. The truth-times-info score combines them. Per-category and per-prompt breakdowns show where the capability fails. The authors say the large differences between models exceed the 2-6% disagreement range.

The support is partial. The disagreement analysis shows that the differences between models exceed the evaluation noise. The threshold of 0.5 is justified by consistency among evaluators. The scalar scores in Appendix B.2 and the thresholded results show similar patterns. The GPT-judge rank ordering is preserved within each family. There is no sensitivity analysis of weighting or of the aggregation method.
BIASED (adversarially written questions that elicit imitative falsehoods; shallow coverage of general knowledge)
PARTIAL-INTERFERENCE (human evaluation by authors; GPT-judge requires OpenAI API fine-tuned models that are not externally available)
PARTIAL (US/English-centric cultural content; adversarially filtered against GPT-3; strict standard rejecting belief-system claims)
